46	// Election is compared against the remote of the push actually being made, so

48	// any OTHER remote — `git push <other> HEAD`, a `git clone -o base` whose

60	func ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote(ctx context.Context) (CheckpointSyncRemote, error) {
61		// Fail closed on an unreadable settings file: election must never
62		// override a checkpoint_push_remote the file may contain but we could
63		// not read, or checkpoints would silently re-route away from the remote
64		// the user configured for isolation.
65		s, err := settings.Load(ctx)
66		if err != nil {
67			return CheckpointSyncRemote{}, fmt.Errorf("cannot read settings to resolve the checkpoint sync remote: %w", err)
68		}
69		if name := s.GetCheckpointPushRemote(); name != "" {
70			if !isConfiguredRemote(ctx, name) {
71				return CheckpointSyncRemote{}, fmt.Errorf(
72					"checkpoint_push_remote %q is not a configured git remote; checkpoint sync disabled until fixed", name)
73			}
74			return CheckpointSyncRemote{Name: name, Source: SyncRemoteSourceConfig}, nil
75		}
76	
77		remotes := configuredRemotesInConfigOrder(ctx)
78		switch {
79		case len(remotes) == 0:
80			return CheckpointSyncRemote{}, nil
81		case slices.Contains(remotes, "origin"):
82			return CheckpointSyncRemote{Name: "origin", Source: SyncRemoteSourceDefault}, nil
83		case len(remotes) == 1:
84			return CheckpointSyncRemote{Name: remotes[0], Source: SyncRemoteSourceSole}, nil

92	// checkpoint sync remote — including raw-URL pushes (git passes the URL as

102				slog.String("error", err.Error()))
103			return false
104		}
105		if syncRemote.Name == "" || syncRemote.Name != pushRemote {
106			logging.Debug(ctx, "checkpoint sync skipped: push remote is not the checkpoint sync remote",
107				slog.String("push_remote", pushRemote),
108				slog.String("checkpoint_sync_remote", syncRemote.Name))

118	func configuredRemotesInConfigOrder(ctx context.Context) []string {
119		out, err := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", "config", "--local", "--get-regexp", `^remote\..*\.url$`).Output()
120		if err != nil {
121			return nil
122		}
123		var names []string
124		seen := map[string]bool{}
125		for _, line := range strings.Split(strings.TrimSpace(string(out)), "\n") {
126			// line: "remote.<name>.url <url>"; <name> may contain dots, so trim
127			// the fixed prefix and the ".url <value>" suffix instead of splitting.

135			}
136			seen[name] = true
137			names = append(names, name)
138		}

12	// refsPushDestination is the single place checkpoint refs are pushed to.
13	type refsPushDestination struct {
14		// target is passed to git push and to the recovery fetch: a remote name, or a URL.
15		target string
16		// checkpointRemote records that target came from a configured
17		// checkpoint_remote. It cannot be recovered from target's shape — a
18		// resolved push URL is URL-shaped too — and it decides both how the
19		// destination is named and whether the "a checkpoint remote is configured"
20		// hint applies.
21		checkpointRemote bool
22		// ignoredPushURLs counts the push URLs of a multi-URL remote that will NOT
23		// receive checkpoint refs. Zero in every single-destination topology.
24		ignoredPushURLs int
25	}
26	
27	// resolveRefsPushDestination picks the single destination for checkpoint-ref
28	// pushes.
29	//
30	// Checkpoint refs need ONE deterministic destination, because the push-discovery
31	// queue records only a ref (`{"ref": …}`) with no per-destination state: a ref is
32	// removed from the queue once "the push" succeeds, so "the push" has to mean one
33	// place. Relying on git's fan-out across a remote's several push URLs breaks that
34	// in both directions — a single failing URL fails the whole invocation and no ref
35	// unqueues even though some URLs took it, and an unreachable FIRST URL makes git
36	// die() before it reaches any later URL at all.
37	//
38	// So when a remote carries more than one push URL we target its first push URL
39	// directly (the one git itself would push to first) and ignore the rest. The
40	// recovery fetch in fetchAndRebaseRefCommon uses the same target, so — unlike the
41	// fan-out path, which reconciled the remote's FETCH url while pushing to its
42	// pushurls — the URL we reconcile is finally the URL we push to.
43	//
44	// Consequences, deliberately accepted:
45	//   - Checkpoint refs live in exactly one repository. Cloning that repository
46	//     resolves them (its url becomes the clone's fetch URL); cloning a different
47	//     mirror of the same code does not. Mirroring checkpoints to several
48	//     repositories is what checkpoint_remote is for.
49	//   - A first push URL that REJECTS a ref (non-fast-forward) no longer lets later
50	//     URLs receive it. git would have carried on to them; we stop. That is the
51	//     price of a deterministic destination, and it is the case the queue can
52	//     actually reason about.
53	//
54	// The git-branch backend deliberately keeps git's fan-out: its v1 branch is a
55	// single shared ref with no queue to keep coherent, and mirroring it to every
56	// push URL is behavior users configure their remotes for.
57	//
58	// A single push URL keeps the remote NAME as the target rather than resolving it
59	// to a URL, so the overwhelmingly common topology behaves exactly as before —
60	// remote-tracking refs still update, output still says "origin", and no
61	// URL-keyed promisor config appears.
62	//
63	// Call this only once there is something to push: it spawns `git remote get-url`
64	// and its result is unused on an empty queue.
65	func resolveRefsPushDestination(ctx context.Context, ps pushSettings) refsPushDestination {
66		target := ps.pushTarget()
67	
68		// A configured checkpoint_remote, or a push straight to a URL (git hands the
69		// hook a bare URL verbatim), is already a single explicit destination.
70		if ps.hasCheckpointURL() || remote.IsURL(target) {
71			return refsPushDestination{target: target, checkpointRemote: ps.hasCheckpointURL()}
72		}
73	
74		urls, err := remote.GetPushURLs(ctx, target)
75		if err != nil {
76			// Not a configured remote, or git could not report its URLs. Keep the
77			// target as given; the push itself will report any real problem.
78			logging.Debug(ctx, "git-refs push: could not enumerate push URLs; using target as given",
79				slog.String("target", target),
80				slog.String("error", err.Error()),
81			)
82		}
83		if len(urls) < 2 {
84			return refsPushDestination{target: target}
85		}
86		return refsPushDestination{target: urls[0], ignoredPushURLs: len(urls) - 1}
87	}

89	// display names the destination for progress and warning output.
90	//
91	// Deliberately not displayPushTarget: that maps ANY URL to the literal words
92	// "checkpoint remote", which was only ever true because a URL target implied a
93	// configured checkpoint_remote. A push URL we resolved ourselves is URL-shaped
94	// but is not a checkpoint remote, so it is named by its (redacted) URL.
95	func (d refsPushDestination) display() string {
96		switch {
97		case d.checkpointRemote:
98			return "checkpoint remote"
99		case d.ignoredPushURLs > 0:
100			return fmt.Sprintf("%s (first of %d push URLs)", remote.RedactURLOrPath(d.target), d.ignoredPushURLs+1)
101		default:
102			return remote.RedactURLOrPath(d.target)
103		}
104	}
105	
106	// warnIgnoredPushURLs tells the user that checkpoint refs are going to one URL of
107	// a multi-URL remote — otherwise the choice is invisible and looks like the other
108	// mirrors silently lost their checkpoints. Call it only when there are refs to
109	// push, so a no-op push stays quiet.
110	func (d refsPushDestination) warnIgnoredPushURLs(ctx context.Context) {
111		if d.ignoredPushURLs == 0 {
112			return
113		}
114		fmt.Fprintf(stderrWriter, "[entire] Checkpoints go to one repository: %s. %d other push URL(s) of this remote will not receive them.\n",
115			d.display(), d.ignoredPushURLs)
116		fmt.Fprintln(stderrWriter, "[entire] To store checkpoints in a specific repository instead, set checkpoint_remote in .entire/settings.json.")

## [0.10.0] - 2026-08-12

- Long-deprecated commands are removed: `entire reset` (use `entire clean`), `entire rewind` and `entire checkpoint rewind`, and the hidden top-level `resume` / `attach` / `explain` / `trace` shortcuts (use the `session`, `checkpoint`, and `doctor` subcommands) ([#1747](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1747))

In a repo with several remotes, pushing anywhere previously copied session transcripts there ([#1893](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1893), [#1905](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1905), [#1898](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1898))

## Problem

On the git-refs backend, cross-machine **enumeration** never worked in the default setup: `ListCheckpointRefsOnRemote` returned nothing unless a dedicated `checkpoint_remote` was configured (scoped out when remote enumeration was introduced in #1771). A fresh clone running `checkpoint list` or the branch view saw zero checkpoints — even though known-ID hydration (`explain` on a commit with a trailer) worked fine. Repos with a dedicated store (like this one) never hit the gap, which is why it went unnoticed.

## Change

When no dedicated store is configured, discovery now ls-remotes the checkpoint read candidates — the elected sync remote (per #1893's election), then `origin` — for `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` and **merges the listings** (union, deduped): refs historically landed on whichever remote the pre-push hook fired for, so disjoint listings across remotes are realistic and first-non-empty would shadow one side. Known-ID hydration consumes the same election result: a fail-open `origin` read may satisfy a fetch, but an `origin` miss cannot falsely certify global absence when election failed.

- **Best-effort:** each candidate gets its own short budget, so a hung leader cannot starve the rest. Partial failure returns reachable results; total failure triggers the existing warning and degrades to a local-only listing.
- **Bounded hydration:** one chain-wide deadline covers all known-ID fetch candidates rather than granting each candidate a fresh full timeout.
- **Cheap:** ls-remote is names-only; runs only on enumeration paths that opt in (`WithRemoteListDiscovery`), never in hooks.
- **Token-aware:** candidate URLs resolve through `remote.FetchURL` with the new `LeadReadRemote` option, preserving the `ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN`-with-SSH-origin case.
- Dedicated `checkpoint_remote` behavior is byte-identical.

## Notes for reviewers

- `strategy.CheckpointReadRemotes` / `CheckpointReadRemotesWithElection` is the candidate resolver. Enumeration uses the ordered candidates; ref hydration consumes the election result as well so a fail-open `origin` read cannot falsely certify global absence. #1951 remains the broader read-side follow-up for metadata, policy, resume, and other read paths.

Future restacks must preserve: the checkpoint-fetch authority gate, malformed `checkpoint_remote` gates, non-authoritative candidate rejection, transport-failure handling, and discovery settings-load handling. I've got the complete picture now. Everything verified against latest main (`ec5593200`), the merged commit for #1893, both PR branches, and the v0.10.0 release.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The system here has two separable decisions that are easy to conflate: **election** (which one remote *should* carry checkpoints — the 4-tier precedence you quoted) and the **gate** (checkpoints only ride a push whose target *equals* the elected remote; pushes to any other remote are silent no-ops for checkpoint data). The reporter's complaint is about the gate, not the election.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Verdict: #1893 did not break the stated logic — but it did intentionally change behavior the reporter may be relying on

The election in `strategy/checkpoint_sync_remote.go:60-88` implements your 4 tiers exactly: `checkpoint_push_remote` (fail-closed if the named remote doesn't exist) → `origin` → sole remote → first in `.git/config` order. Unit tests cover every tier, including `TestResolveCheckpointSyncRemote_SoleRemote` and `_FirstInConfigOrder`.

So the answer depends on which topology the reporter has:

**Sole remote not named `origin` (e.g. just `gh`)** — **not broken.** Tier 3 elects it, the gate passes (`checkpointSyncAllowedForRemote` compares the hook's remote name against the elected name), and checkpoints push. If the reporter has exactly one remote and checkpoints stopped, that would be a real bug worth a repro — but I traced the full pre-push path and found no origin-dependence on the write side.

**`origin` exists but they push to a different remote (fork/mirror workflow), or multiple remotes with no origin where they push a non-first remote** — **this is the real change, and it's deliberate.** Pre-#1893, checkpoints piggy-backed on *every* push to *any* remote. Since v0.10.0 (released Aug 12 — the day before the report; #1893 was in it), pushes to non-elected remotes carry nothing. This is asserted as intended behavior by `TestCheckpointSyncRemote_DefaultElection_OnlyOriginReceivesCheckpoints`, and the changelog says it outright: *"Checkpoints now sync to a single elected remote instead of every remote you push to."* Checkpoints aren't lost — they queue locally (push-discovery queue on git-refs; the v1 branch stays ahead on git-branch) and drain when the elected remote is eventually pushed. `entire status` names the elected destination and shows the unpushed count.

The supported answer for "I push to a remote that isn't origin" is `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote: "<that remote>"`.

## Where the open PRs fit

**Neither #1956 nor #1951 changes the write gate.** They fix the *read* side, which is what currently makes the `checkpoint_push_remote` remedy half-broken on v0.10.0: reads (resume, explain, metadata fetch, discovery) still hardcode origin's remote-tracking refs (`strategy/common.go:551,1069,1604-1631`, `metadata_reconcile.go:82`), so checkpoints written to a non-origin elected remote can't be read back. #1893's own doc comment admitted this gap.

- **#1956** (base of the stack): git-refs checkpoint *discovery* without a dedicated `checkpoint_remote` — ls-remotes the read candidates (elected remote, then origin) and unions the listings. Fixes a pre-#1893 gap from #1771.
- **#1951** (stacked on #1956): the full "writes confine; reads search" rework — every read path consults elected-first-then-origin, fails *open* for reads (vs. fail-closed writes), and confines local-ref advancement to the elected remote only. It also hardens the election helpers with an explicit `cmd.Dir = worktreeRoot`.

#1951's reviewer notes state the residual explicitly: *"The remaining objection — silent no-op on pushes to other remotes — still stands; whether to revisit the tracking tier is a product call, now unblocked from the read side."*

## What I'd tell the reporter

1. Ask which topology they have (`git remote -v`). If it's a **sole** non-origin remote, checkpoints should still push on v0.10.0 — if they observably don't, we want that repro.
2. If origin coexists with their push remote: yes, intentional as of v0.10.0; set `checkpoint_push_remote` to their push remote. Honest caveat until #1956/#1951 merge: reads (resume/explain from another clone, cross-machine discovery) still assume origin, so the config makes writes correct now and reads correct once the stack lands.
3. The open product question — whether pushes to non-elected remotes should *redirect* checkpoint data to the elected remote instead of no-op'ing (which would restore "my checkpoints always leave the machine" without restoring the multi-remote transcript-spraying #1893 was fixing) — is not addressed by any of the three PRs. If the reporter's workflow is "never push the elected remote," that redirect (or at least a one-line stderr hint during the gated push, rather than only a debug log) might be worth considering; today the skip is visible only in `entire status` and debug logs.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The gate compares against *the push actually being made* rather than pushing to the elected remote out-of-band — a deliberate choice: a pre-push hook that pushes to a *different* remote than the one the user asked for would surprise users, hit auth prompts for a remote they didn't invoke, and turn `git push fork` into network traffic to origin. The cost is exactly this support question: checkpoints stall until the elected remote is pushed.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Yes — that order is exactly what's implemented, verified against `strategy/checkpoint_sync_remote.go:60-88` on latest main:

1. `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote` — and it's genuinely fail-closed: if the named remote isn't configured in git, checkpoint sync is **disabled entirely with an error**, it does not fall through to origin (`checkpoint_sync_remote.go:69-75`)

Two extra properties worth knowing when explaining it: an unreadable settings file also fails closed (so a broken file can't silently re-route checkpoints away from a configured remote), and branch tracking config (`branch.<name>.remote`, `remote.pushDefault`) deliberately **never** participates in the election.

## How to set it

There's no CLI flag for it — `entire configure` doesn't expose it, so it's a JSON edit. Two file options, both merged by `settings.Load`:

**Personal, per-clone (gitignored)** — `.entire/settings.local.json`. This is the right place for the reporter, since "what I named my remote" is a personal clone-level fact, not something to impose on other contributors:

```json
{
  "strategy_options": {
    "checkpoint_push_remote": "gh"
  }
}
```

**Shared/committed** — the same block in `.entire/settings.json`, if the whole team pushes to the same non-origin remote.

Then verify with `entire status` — since #1893 it names the elected destination and its source, so they should see the remote reported with source `config` (and `entire status --json` exposes `checkpoint_sync_remote` / `checkpoint_sync_remote_source`). If they typo the remote name, the fail-closed error surfaces there too, rather than checkpoints silently going somewhere else.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The settings merge in `loadMergedSettings` (`settings.go:518-555`) layers local over shared via `mergeJSON`, and both files funnel through the same `GetCheckpointPushRemote()` accessor — so the local file can override just this one key without duplicating the rest of `strategy_options`. This is also why the fail-closed rule reads the settings *file* error as fatal: election runs inside the pre-push hook, where guessing on unreadable config would mean pushing transcripts to a remote the user may have explicitly routed away from.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

## Why Order Matters

**"I'll write tests after to verify it works"**

Tests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:
- Might test wrong thing
- Might test implementation, not behavior
- Might miss edge cases you forgot
- You never saw it catch the bug

Test-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.

**"I already manually tested all the edge cases"**

Manual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:
- No record of what you tested
- Can't re-run when code changes
- Easy to forget cases under pressure
- "It worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive

Automated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.

**"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful"**

Sunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:
- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)
- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)

The "waste" is keeping code you can't trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.

**"TDD is dogmatic, being pragmatic means adapting"**

TDD IS pragmatic:
- Finds bugs before commit (faster than debugging after)
- Prevents regressions (tests catch breaks immediately)
- Documents behavior (tests show how to use code)
- Enables refactoring (change freely, tests catch breaks)

"Pragmatic" shortcuts = debugging in production = slower.

**"Tests after achieve the same goals - it's spirit not ritual"**

No. Tests-after answer "What does this do?" Tests-first answer "What should this do?"

Tests-after are biased by your implementation. You test what you built, not what's required. You verify remembered edge cases, not discovered ones.

Tests-first force edge case discovery before implementing. Tests-after verify you remembered everything (you didn't).

30 minutes of tests after ≠ TDD. You get coverage, lose proof tests work.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests passing immediately prove nothing. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals" | Tests-after = "what does this do?" Tests-first = "what should this do?" |
| "Already manually tested" | Ad-hoc ≠ systematic. No record, can't re-run. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy. Keeping unverified code is technical debt. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD faster than debugging. Pragmatic = test-first. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Testing Anti-Patterns

When adding mocks or test utilities, read @testing-anti-patterns.md to avoid common pitfalls:
- Testing mock behavior instead of real behavior
- Adding test-only methods to production classes
- Mocking without understanding dependencies

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

gh pr create --title "fix(strategy): hint on gated pre-push when checkpoints are waiting" --body "## Problem

Since the single-remote gate (ENT-1451, shipped in v0.10.0), a push to a non-elected remote silently stops carrying checkpoints. A user whose habitual push remote loses the default election to a dormant \`origin\` sees checkpoints strand locally with **no signal in the push output** — the skip only shows in \`entire status\` and the debug log. The first real user hit this within a day of the release (\"I have a bunch of repos where the git remote I push to isn't called origin. It looks like this means I no longer push checkpoints. Is that intentional?\").

## Change

The pre-push hook prints a two-line stderr hint on a gated push:

\`\`\`
[entire] 3 checkpoint(s) are waiting to sync to \"origin\", this repo's checkpoint sync remote; this push to \"fork\" does not carry them.
[entire] To sync checkpoints to \"fork\" instead, set strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote to \"fork\" in .entire/settings.json.
\`\`\`

It stays quiet when:
- the election was **explicit** (a configured \`checkpoint_push_remote\` is a decision already made — gated pushes are intentional, no nagging),
- the push target is a **raw URL** (the setting takes a remote name; nothing actionable to suggest),
- **nothing is waiting** (a gated push after checkpoints already synced stays clean),
- the **election failed** (the fail-closed path already warns through the gate).

Fully local — reuses \`CountUnpushedCheckpoints\` (push-queue length on git-refs, v1-ahead count on git-branch), no network in the hook.

## Testing

- Unit: \`TestHintGatedCheckpointSync\` covers the hint and all four silence conditions.
- Integration: \`assertSingleRemoteRouting\` now asserts the gated leg's output on both backends — hint present for the default and tracking-config elections, absent for the explicit \`checkpoint_push_remote\` override. New \`RunPrePushOutput\` harness variant captures hook output.
- \`mise run fmt\`, \`mise run lint\` (0 issues), full unit suite (8837 pass), and the \`TestCheckpointSyncRemote\` integration slice all green.

## Non-goals

Whether the election itself should gain a tracking tier (so a habitually-pushed remote can win over a dormant origin without config) stays the product call deferred in #1893/#1951 — this PR only makes the existing gate self-explaining.
